lead: This unit is about circuits that store energy in inductors and capacitors and exchange it at one frequency, and about coils that share magnetic flux. It covers series and parallel resonance, Q, bandwidth and selectivity, frequency response, locus diagrams, then self and mutual inductance, the dot convention, ideal and linear transformers and magnetic circuits. After it you can find f₀, Q and bandwidth, draw a current locus, write coupled-coil equations with the right signs, use transformer ratios and solve series and parallel magnetic circuits.
about: The unit starts with series resonance, where X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub> and the current peaks, and its dual, parallel resonance, where the tank impedance peaks. Quality factor then ties both to bandwidth and selectivity, and the frequency-response chapter draws the RC and RLC shapes. Locus diagrams show the same circuits as one parameter varies. The second half turns to magnetism: self and mutual inductance and the coefficient of coupling, the dot convention for coupled coils, ideal and linear transformers, and magnetic circuits with MMF, flux and reluctance.

chapters.idea: Series resonance is the frequency where inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, leaving only R and giving maximum current.
chapters.depth: Cover the series RLC circuit: Z = R + j(X_L − X_C), X_L = ωL, X_C = 1/(ωC). At resonance X_L = X_C, so Z = R, phase is zero, current is maximum. Derive ω₀ = 1/√(LC) and f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)); define ω in rad/s and f in Hz. Show the resonance curve and half-power points. Define Q for series RLC: Q = ω₀L/R = 1/(ω₀CR) = (1/R)√(L/C). Show voltage magnification V_L = V_C = QV at resonance. Mention the names acceptor circuit and voltage resonance. Some syllabi call f₀ the natural frequency; give damping ratio ζ = R/(2ω₀L) = 1/(2Q) only as a bridge, and leave overdamped, critically damped and underdamped response to Unit 5. Keep the treatment at phasor level.

figure.aria: Normalised current against normalised frequency for series RLC circuits with Q = 3 and Q = 10; the Q = 10 curve peaks sharply at 1.

chapters.example: A series RLC circuit has R = 10 Ω, L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF, with a 10 V rms source at resonance. Find f₀, Q, bandwidth and the voltage across the capacitor. f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1591.5 Hz, Q = (1/R)√(L/C) = 10, bandwidth = f₀/Q = 159.2 Hz. At resonance X_L = X_C = 100 Ω, so I = 10/10 = 1 A and V_C = I X_C = 100 V.
chapters.trap: Do not set X_L = X_C at any frequency other than ω₀; do not use f in place of ω in Q = ω₀L/R; V_L and V_C cancel in the source loop but each can be Q times the source voltage.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for R, L, C V-I relations; Unit 3 for impedance, phasors and series AC circuits.
chapters.leave: Transient ringing and damping ratio cases go to Unit 5; parallel resonance goes to 4.2; detailed filter design goes to 4.4.

chapters.idea: Parallel resonance is the frequency where susceptances cancel, so a parallel tank presents maximum impedance and minimum supply current.
chapters.depth: Cover the ideal parallel RLC circuit: Y = 1/R + j(ωC − 1/(ωL)); at resonance ωC = 1/(ωL), Y = 1/R, Z = R is maximum, supply current is minimum. Use the same ω₀ = 1/√(LC). Define Q for parallel RLC: Q = R/(ω₀L) = ω₀CR = R√(C/L). Explain current magnification: inductor and capacitor currents can be Q times the supply current. Then cover the practical tank: a coil of resistance r in parallel with C; give the resonance condition and dynamic resistance in words, with f₀ = (1/(2π))√(1/(LC) − (r/L)²) for the low-loss case. Mention the names rejector circuit and current resonance. Keep phasor level.

figure.aria: Normalised impedance magnitude against frequency for parallel RLC circuits; impedance is maximum at f₀, and the Q = 10 circuit is sharper than the Q = 3 circuit.

chapters.example: A parallel RLC circuit has R = 1 kΩ, L = 10 mH and C = 1 µF, with a 10 V rms source. Find f₀, Q, bandwidth, supply current and circulating current at resonance. f₀ = 1591.5 Hz, Q = R/(ω₀L) = 10, bandwidth = 159.2 Hz. At resonance Z = R = 1 kΩ, so supply current = 10/1000 = 10 mA. Inductor current = 10/(ω₀L) = 10/100 = 100 mA, which is Q times the supply current.
chapters.trap: Ideal parallel resonance differs from a practical coil tank because coil resistance shifts the resonant frequency. Impedance is maximum at resonance, not minimum; supply current is minimum, but coil and capacitor currents are large.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for the resonance condition and Q; Unit 3 for admittance and parallel AC circuits.
chapters.leave: Q–bandwidth derivation goes to 4.3; practical coil loss beyond the low-loss formula is for advanced study; transient response goes to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Q measures stored energy per cycle lost, and it fixes both bandwidth and selectivity: high Q means narrow bandwidth and sharp selectivity.
chapters.depth: Define Q from energy: Q = 2π × (peak energy stored)/(energy lost per cycle). Give series Q = ω₀L/R = 1/(ω₀CR) and parallel Q = R/(ω₀L) = ω₀CR. Define bandwidth as f₂ − f₁, the half-power frequencies where power is half maximum and voltage or current is 1/√2 of maximum. Derive BW = f₀/Q and ω_BW = ω₀/Q. Define selectivity as the ability to separate a wanted frequency from nearby unwanted ones; smaller BW/f₀ means higher selectivity. Give high-Q approximations f₁ ≈ f₀ − BW/2 and f₂ ≈ f₀ + BW/2, valid for Q ≥ 10. Link ζ = 1/(2Q) for series RLC but leave its transient use to Unit 5.

figure.aria: Selectivity curves for Q = 5, 20 and 50; higher Q gives a narrower peak and a smaller bandwidth around f₀.

chapters.example: A series RLC circuit has f₀ = 1 kHz and Q = 50. Find the bandwidth, the half-power frequencies and the selectivity ratio. BW = f₀/Q = 1000/50 = 20 Hz. For Q ≥ 10, f₁ ≈ 990 Hz and f₂ ≈ 1010 Hz. Selectivity ratio = BW/f₀ = 0.02, or 2%.
chapters.trap: Bandwidth and Q are inversely related; do not mix Hz and rad/s; series and parallel Q formulas use R in reciprocal ways; f₁,₂ = f₀ ± BW/2 is only a high-Q approximation.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.1 and 4.2 for series and parallel Q; Unit 3 for AC power and the half-power idea.
chapters.leave: Damping ratio and time response go to Unit 5; filter order and Bode design go to 4.4; two-port Q is not needed.

chapters.idea: Frequency response shows how gain and phase change with frequency; RC gives a first-order cutoff and RLC gives a band-pass peak set by Q.
chapters.depth: Cover first-order RC low-pass H(jω) = 1/(1 + jωRC) and high-pass H(jω) = jωRC/(1 + jωRC). Define cutoff ω_c = 1/RC, f_c = 1/(2πRC), the −3 dB point, gain 0.707, phase −45° for low-pass at cutoff, and slope ±20 dB/decade. State in one line that first-order RL circuits have the same form. Cover series RLC band-pass response from the resistor voltage: gain peaks at f₀, half-power points define bandwidth, phase goes from +90° to −90°. Show magnitude plots; no full Bode construction needed. Mention TV tuning and frequency-selective filters as applications.

figure.aria: Frequency response: RC low-pass falls after cutoff, RC high-pass rises to cutoff, and the RLC band-pass peaks at resonance.

chapters.example: An RC low-pass filter has R = 1 kΩ and C = 100 nF. (a) Find f_c. (b) Find gain and phase at 1 kHz. (c) A series RLC band-pass with f₀ = 1 kHz and Q = 10: find its bandwidth. f_c = 1/(2πRC) = 1591.5 Hz. At 1 kHz, f/f_c = 0.628, gain = 1/√(1 + 0.628²) = 0.847, phase = −32.1°. For the RLC band-pass, BW = f₀/Q = 100 Hz.
chapters.trap: The −3 dB point is 0.707 of maximum, not half; use ω = 2πf consistently; in RLC the output across R peaks at f₀, but output across C or L peaks at other frequencies.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 for phasors and impedance; Chapters 4.1–4.3 for resonance, Q and bandwidth.
chapters.leave: Laplace transfer functions, poles and zeros go to Unit 5; two-port transfer functions go to Unit 6; full Bode plotting can be left to lab.

chapters.idea: The tip of the current phasor traces a circle as R, X or the frequency varies.
A changing current in a coil creates self-induced voltage; it also links a nearby coil and creates mutual voltage, with k measuring how much flux is shared.
chapters.depth: Define self-inductance L = NΦ/i and self-induced emf e = L di/dt, with sign from Lenz. Define mutual inductance M = N₂Φ₂₁/i₁ and mutual emf e₂ = M di₁/dt. Define coefficient of coupling k = M/√(L₁L₂), with 0 ≤ k ≤ 1; k = 1 means all flux links both coils. Explain leakage flux and loose or tight coupling. Give units: L₁ and L₂ in henry (H), M in henry, k dimensionless. Give M = k√(L₁L₂). Keep dot signs for 4.6.

figure.aria: Current change in coil 1 creates total flux; the shared part links coil 2 and induces e₂ = M di₁/dt.

chapters.example: Two coils have L₁ = 4 H, L₂ = 1 H and k = 0.5. Find M. If the current in coil 1 changes at 2 A/s, find the induced voltage in coil 2 and the self-induced voltage in coil 1. M = k√(L₁L₂) = 0.5√4 = 1 H. e₂ = M di₁/dt = 1 × 2 = 2 V. e₁ = L₁ di₁/dt = 4 × 2 = 8 V.
chapters.trap: M is not k(L₁ + L₂); k cannot exceed 1; mutual voltage depends on current change in the other coil, not on the coil's own current; M can be zero even when coils are near if their fluxes do not link.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for the inductor relation v = L di/dt; Unit 3 for phasor AC behaviour of inductors.
chapters.leave: Dot convention and sign rules go to 4.6; transformer voltage and current ratios go to 4.7; magnetic reluctance calculation of L goes to 4.8.

chapters.idea: The dot convention fixes the sign of the mutual term: currents entering dotted terminals produce aiding flux, and KVL uses +M or −M accordingly.
chapters.depth: State the dot rule: if both currents enter dotted terminals, the mutual flux aids the self-flux and the mutual voltage at the dotted terminal has the same sign as the self-induced voltage; if one enters and one leaves, the mutual term is negative. Write KVL for two coupled meshes with ±M di/dt terms. Cover series aiding L_eq = L₁ + L₂ + 2M and series opposing L_eq = L₁ + L₂ − 2M. Give parallel aiding and opposing equivalent formulas in terms of L₁, L₂ and M; show that M ≤ √(L₁L₂) keeps the equivalent positive. Use dot marks on circuit diagrams and define dotted terminal.

figure.aria: Decision tree for series coupled coils: currents entering the same dot give aiding flux and +2M; opposite dots give −2M.

chapters.example: Two coils have L₁ = 2 H, L₂ = 3 H and M = 1 H. They are connected in series. Find the equivalent inductance when their fluxes aid and when they oppose. Aiding: L_eq = 2 + 3 + 2(1) = 7 H. Opposing: L_eq = 2 + 3 − 2(1) = 3 H. If current enters the dot of coil 1 and leaves the dot of coil 2, the opposing value 3 H applies.
chapters.trap: The dot is a terminal mark, not a component; dots on the same side do not always mean aiding—current directions decide. The series mutual term is 2M, not M.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.5 for M and k; Unit 1 for KVL; Unit 2 for mesh analysis.
chapters.leave: Transformer models go to 4.7; magnetic circuit flux paths go to 4.8; s-domain coupled coils go to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: An ideal transformer gives lossless voltage, current and impedance scaling by turns ratio; a linear transformer is a coupled-coil model with finite magnetizing inductance.
chapters.depth: Ideal transformer: N₁ and N₂ turns; n = N₂/N₁; V₂/V₁ = n; I₂/I₁ = 1/n with dots and a load; power in = power out; input impedance Z_in = (N₁/N₂)² Z_L. State ideal assumptions: no winding resistance, no core loss, infinite permeability, k = 1. Linear transformer: two coupled coils with finite L₁, L₂ and M; write mesh equations and input impedance Z_in = jωL₁ + (ωM)²/(jωL₂ + Z_L) for the usual dot arrangement; explain magnetizing current. Mention use in chargers and distribution. Keep steady AC.

figure.aria: Ideal transformer flow: primary voltage sets core flux, secondary voltage is n times primary, and load current reflects to primary divided by n.

chapters.example: An ideal transformer has N₁ = 500 turns, N₂ = 100 turns, primary voltage 230 V rms and a 10 Ω load on the secondary. Find V₂, I₂, I₁ and Z_in. n = N₂/N₁ = 0.2, so V₂ = 0.2 × 230 = 46 V. I₂ = 46/10 = 4.6 A. I₁ = n I₂ = 0.2 × 4.6 = 0.92 A. Z_in = (N₁/N₂)² × 10 = 25 × 10 = 250 Ω.
chapters.trap: Turns ratio direction: n = N₂/N₁ for voltage, but current ratio is inverse. Impedance is scaled by n², not n. An ideal transformer is the limiting case, not a linear transformer with finite L.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.5 and 4.6 for M and dots; Unit 3 for AC impedance.
chapters.leave: Core reluctance and flux go to 4.8; s-domain transformer step response goes to Unit 5; three-phase transformer connections go to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A magnetic circuit is driven by MMF = NI and opposed by reluctance R = l/(μA), so flux Φ = MMF/R, like Ohm's law.
chapters.depth: Define MMF F = NI in ampere-turns, flux Φ in weber, reluctance R = l/(μA) in A/Wb, permeability μ = μ₀μ_r, and μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m. Give B = Φ/A, H = NI/l and B = μH. Explain the magnetic Ohm's law analogy: MMF ↔ voltage, flux ↔ current, reluctance ↔ resistance. Cover series magnetic circuits: reluctances add; parallel paths: flux divides and reluctances combine like parallel resistors. Show that an air gap has large reluctance and controls flux. Ignore fringing and saturation unless stated.

figure.aria: Magnetic circuit flow: MMF drives flux through series core and air-gap reluctances.

chapters.example: A ring core has mean core length 0.4 m, cross-section 4×10⁻⁴ m², relative permeability 500, air gap 1 mm and N = 500 turns carrying 2 A. Find core reluctance, gap reluctance, flux and flux density. R_c = 0.4/(μ₀×500×4×10⁻⁴) = 1.59×10⁶ A/Wb. R_g = 1×10⁻³/(μ₀×4×10⁻⁴) = 1.99×10⁶ A/Wb. MMF = 500 × 2 = 1000 A. Φ = 1000/(3.58×10⁶) = 2.79×10⁻⁴ Wb. B = Φ/A = 0.698 T.
chapters.trap: Air-gap reluctance uses μ₀, not μ₀μ_r; gap length must be in metres; reluctance has the same series and parallel rules as resistance, but flux is not current and MMF is not voltage.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for Ohm's law and series/parallel resistors; basic area and length units.
chapters.leave: Transformer action and turns ratio go to 4.7; inductance from reluctance L = N²/R can be mentioned but is left to 4.5; hysteresis and eddy current losses are outside this unit.
